flashcards.front: What is the primary OpenAI API surface for new projects?
flashcards.back: The **Responses API**. The docs say Responses is recommended for all new projects; Chat Completions is still supported, and the Assistants API was sunset on 2026-08-26.

flashcards.front: What does `output_text` give you?
flashcards.back: An SDK convenience that joins the text of all message items in `response.output`.

flashcards.front: What type is `response.output`?
flashcards.back: An **array of items**: messages, reasoning items, function calls, hosted tool calls and more.

flashcards.front: Where do system-level rules go in a Responses API call?
flashcards.back: In `instructions`, which takes priority over `input` (or in a `developer` message, which outranks `user` messages). Instructions apply only to the current request.

flashcards.front: What does streaming improve?
flashcards.back: Perceived latency (time to first token). Total generation time and cost are about the same.

flashcards.front: Four ways to manage conversation state?
flashcards.back: Manual history, `previous_response_id` chaining, the Conversations API, and choosing `store` true/false.

flashcards.front: Does `previous_response_id` make earlier turns free?
flashcards.back: No. All prior input tokens in the chain are still billed as input.

flashcards.front: When use the Conversations API?
flashcards.back: For durable state reused across sessions, devices or jobs.

flashcards.front: Default retention for stored response objects?
flashcards.back: 30 days by default (per the docs). `store=false` disables storage. Conversation objects and their items are not subject to the 30-day TTL.

flashcards.front: Replaying manual history with a reasoning model: what must you include?
flashcards.back: Every output item, including reasoning items, so the model keeps its context.

flashcards.front: What does higher reasoning effort cost?
flashcards.back: More reasoning tokens (billed as output, reported in `usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`) and more latency, in exchange for better results on hard problems.

flashcards.front: How should you pick between GPT models?
flashcards.back: Use evals: the cheapest model and lowest reasoning effort that meet your quality bar.

flashcards.front: Status of the Assistants API?
flashcards.back: **Sunset on 2026-08-26** and no longer available. Migrate to the Responses API: Threads → Conversations, Runs → Responses, Run steps → Items.

flashcards.front: Which reasoning effort values exist, and are they the same for every model?
flashcards.back: Values can include `none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`, but **support is per model**. GPT-6 Astra rejects `none` with HTTP 400; GPT-6.1 Sol supports neither `none` nor `minimal`.

flashcards.front: What does `max_output_tokens` cover on a reasoning model?
flashcards.back: Reasoning tokens **plus** visible output. Hitting it returns `status: "incomplete"` (reason `max_output_tokens`), possibly with no visible text.

flashcards.front: Why pin a dated model snapshot in production?
flashcards.back: Aliases can move to newer versions. A pinned snapshot (e.g. `gpt-5.5-2026-04-23` in the docs) keeps behavior stable until you choose to upgrade after an eval run.

flashcards.front: Name the core Responses streaming events.
flashcards.back: `response.created`, `response.output_text.delta`, `response.completed`, `error`, plus `response.refusal.delta` for refusals and delta events for function-call arguments.

flashcards.front: Are `instructions` carried forward when you chain with `previous_response_id`?
flashcards.back: No. `instructions` apply only to the current request; send them again on each call.

flashcards.front: Assistants → Responses concept mapping?
flashcards.back: Assistants → Prompts (kept in your code), Threads → Conversations, Runs → Responses, Run steps → Items.

flashcards.front: Two ways to compact a long conversation server-side?
flashcards.back: `context_management` with a `compact_threshold` on `/responses` (works with `store=false`), or the stateless `/responses/compact` endpoint, which returns an opaque encrypted item you must not prune.

flashcards.front: Which GPT-6 model does the docs suggest if you are not sure where to start?
flashcards.back: GPT-6 Astra, the flagship for complex reasoning and coding. Sol balances intelligence and cost; Luna suits cost-sensitive, high-volume work.

flashcards.front: Besides type: "function", which fields define a function tool?
flashcards.back: `name`, `description` and `parameters` (a JSON Schema). Add `strict: true` for schema-conformant arguments.

flashcards.front: What links a function result back to the call?
flashcards.back: The `call_id`: send a `function_call_output` item with the same `call_id`.

flashcards.front: When does a function-calling loop end?
flashcards.back: When a response contains no more function_call items. A max-turn cap is only a safety net.

flashcards.front: Model returns three function calls at once. What do you do?
flashcards.back: Run all three (in parallel if safe) and return a function_call_output for **each** call_id.

flashcards.front: `tool_choice` options?
flashcards.back: `auto` (default, zero or more calls), `required` (one or more), a specific function, `allowed_tools` (a subset) or `none`.

flashcards.front: How do you stop the model calling tools in parallel?
flashcards.back: Set `parallel_tool_calls` to false: the model then makes zero or one tool call per turn.

flashcards.front: Best way to return a tool failure?
flashcards.back: A structured error in the output, with what went wrong and a hint for the next step.

flashcards.front: Biggest lever on whether the model picks the right tool?
flashcards.back: A clear, specific tool description (what, when to use, when not to).

flashcards.front: Name five built-in tools in the Responses API tools guide.
flashcards.back: Web search, file search, Code Interpreter, image generation, computer use (the guide also lists shell, skills, tool search and remote MCP). Computer use is not executed by OpenAI: your harness performs its actions.

flashcards.front: What does file search need?
flashcards.back: Your documents uploaded to a **vector store**, referenced by ID in the tool.

flashcards.front: Who executes hosted tools vs function tools?
flashcards.back: Most built-in tools and remote MCP run on OpenAI's side; function tools run in your code. Computer use is the exception: your harness performs the actions.

flashcards.front: Key safety settings for a remote MCP tool?
flashcards.back: Trusted server, restricted allowed tools, least-privilege credentials, `require_approval` for consequential actions.

flashcards.front: Where should a "refunds over $100 need approval" rule live?
flashcards.back: In your code (the refund function or an approval step), not only in the prompt.

flashcards.front: What type is `function_call.arguments`?
flashcards.back: A **JSON string**. Parse it (e.g. `json.loads`) and validate it before running the tool.

flashcards.front: Your function has nothing to return. What do you send?
flashcards.back: Still send a `function_call_output` for the call_id, e.g. `"success"`.

flashcards.front: `tool_choice` with `allowed_tools` does what?
flashcards.back: Restricts calls to a subset of the tools without changing the tools list, so the prompt cache stays intact.

flashcards.front: Soft guideline on how many functions to offer per turn?
flashcards.back: Fewer than 20 available at the start of a turn. Defer large or rarely used sets with tool search.

flashcards.front: Are tool definitions free?
flashcards.back: No. They take up context and are billed as input tokens.

flashcards.front: What is a custom tool?
flashcards.back: `type: "custom"`: takes free-text input, optionally constrained by a Lark or regex grammar. Calls arrive as `custom_tool_call` items with an `input` field.

flashcards.front: How do you restrict web search to certain sites?
flashcards.back: `filters.allowed_domains` (or `blocked_domains`) on the `web_search` tool, without the protocol prefix. Subdomains are included.

flashcards.front: How must web search citations be shown?
flashcards.back: The `url_citation` annotations must be shown as prominent, clickable links.

flashcards.front: Why is `file_search_call.results` null?
flashcards.back: Results are only returned when you pass `include: ["file_search_call.results"]`.

flashcards.front: What happens to an idle Code Interpreter container?
flashcards.back: It expires after about 20 minutes idle and cannot be revived. Create a new one.

flashcards.front: How do you answer a `computer_call`?
flashcards.back: Perform its `actions` in your sandbox, then send `computer_call_output` with the same `call_id` and a `computer_screenshot`.

flashcards.front: What is the `mcp_list_tools` item?
flashcards.back: The server's tool list, returned by the API. Keep it in context so it isn't re-fetched each turn.

flashcards.front: How does remote MCP approval work?
flashcards.back: The model emits `mcp_approval_request`; you send `mcp_approval_response` (request ID + approve true/false) in a new request. One approval covers one call.

flashcards.front: Is the MCP `authorization` token stored between requests?
flashcards.back: No. Send it on every request.

flashcards.front: Extra cost per remote MCP tool call?
flashcards.back: None beyond tokens: "No additional fees apply per tool call."

flashcards.front: What do Structured Outputs guarantee?
flashcards.back: That the response matches your JSON Schema (shape), not that the values are correct.

flashcards.front: Structured Outputs vs JSON mode?
flashcards.back: JSON mode (`text.format: {type: "json_object"}`) only guarantees valid JSON; Structured Outputs (`json_schema` + `strict: true`) enforce your schema.

flashcards.front: How do you make a field optional in a strict schema?
flashcards.back: Keep it in `required` but allow `null` as a type.

flashcards.front: Value of `additionalProperties` in strict schemas?
flashcards.back: `false`.

flashcards.front: Python SDK helper for typed structured output?
flashcards.back: `client.responses.parse(..., text_format=MyPydanticModel)` then `response.output_parsed`.

flashcards.front: TypeScript equivalent?
flashcards.back: The SDK's Zod helper for schema-typed output.

flashcards.front: Besides valid output, what other outcome must extraction code handle?
flashcards.back: A **refusal**: it does not follow the schema and appears as a `refusal` content item, surfaced separately from the parsed object. Also check for `status: "incomplete"`.

flashcards.front: Why include evidence fields (quotes, page numbers) in extraction schemas?
flashcards.back: To verify values and send low-confidence records to human review.

flashcards.front: Do reasoning models need "think step by step"?
flashcards.back: Usually not; they reason internally. Make the prompt specific (task, constraints, format, definition of done) and treat reasoning effort as a tuning knob.

flashcards.front: Where should stable instructions go for caching?
flashcards.back: First, identical every request; variable data last.

flashcards.front: What to do after a model upgrade?
flashcards.back: Re-run evals and read the new model's prompting guidance; behaviour such as length and instruction-following changes.

flashcards.front: Three parts of a clear prompt?
flashcards.back: The task and its goal, constraints (with reasons) and the required output format, plus what "done" means and how to verify it. Add examples for format and edge cases.

flashcards.front: Request shape for Structured Outputs in the Responses API?
flashcards.back: `text: {format: {type: "json_schema", name, strict: true, schema}}`. Chat Completions uses `response_format` instead.

flashcards.front: How do you turn on JSON mode in the Responses API, and what does it guarantee?
flashcards.back: `text.format: {type: "json_object"}`. It guarantees valid JSON only, not that it matches any schema.

flashcards.front: Which JSON Schema keywords are unsupported under strict mode?
flashcards.back: `allOf`, `not`, `if`/`then`/`else`, `dependentRequired`, `dependentSchemas`. Using them with `strict: true` returns an error.

flashcards.front: What must the root of a strict Structured Outputs schema be?
flashcards.back: An object (not an `anyOf`).

flashcards.front: Why is the first request with a new strict schema slower?
flashcards.back: The schema is processed on first use; later requests with the same schema do not pay that extra latency.

flashcards.front: A structured response has `status: "incomplete"`. What could have happened?
flashcards.back: It hit `max_output_tokens` or a `content_filter`, so the JSON may be truncated. Check status before parsing.

flashcards.front: Where do OpenAI's docs now say production prompts should live?
flashcards.back: In your application code, versioned with git, PR review, release tags and feature flags. Prompt objects (`v1/prompts`) are deprecated.

flashcards.front: Where should untrusted content (web pages, emails, tool output) go in a prompt?
flashcards.back: In user messages, never in developer messages or instructions, which carry higher priority.

flashcards.front: How should you treat `reasoning.effort` when quality drops?
flashcards.back: As a tuning knob, not the primary fix. First clarify the task, constraints, format and definition of done.

flashcards.front: Three agent paths in OpenAI's agents guide?
flashcards.back: Responses API (DIY), Agents SDK (loop in your app), Agents API (managed Codex harness in OpenAI's service).

flashcards.front: What does the Agents API manage for you?
flashcards.back: Stored session state, automatic context compaction, multi-agent orchestration (parallel subagents), MCP and tools, and a sandbox that is OpenAI-hosted, self-hosted or from a partner.

flashcards.front: When choose the Agents SDK over the Agents API?
flashcards.back: When you need custom tools and workflows with your own deployment, storage and approvals.

flashcards.front: Install the Python Agents SDK.
flashcards.back: `pip install openai-agents`.

flashcards.front: Agents SDK: who runs the loop?
flashcards.back: The **Runner** (`Runner.run`, `Runner.run_sync`, `Runner.run_streamed`), returning `result.final_output`.

flashcards.front: Decorator for a Python function tool in the SDK?
flashcards.back: `@function_tool`.

flashcards.front: Handoff vs agent-as-tool?
flashcards.back: Handoff transfers the conversation to another agent; agent-as-tool returns a result to the calling agent.

flashcards.front: What is an input guardrail?
flashcards.back: A check on user input that can trip and stop the run early (e.g. off-topic or abusive requests). It runs only on the first agent of a run.

flashcards.front: What do SDK sessions do?
flashcards.back: Store conversation history automatically across runs.

flashcards.front: What does tracing record?
flashcards.back: A trace per workflow, with spans for model calls, tool calls, handoffs and guardrails. On by default.

flashcards.front: When require human approval in an agent?
flashcards.back: Before irreversible or high-impact actions: payments, deletions, external messages, production changes.

flashcards.front: What are sandbox agents?
flashcards.back: SDK agents that work inside a container sandbox, suited to long-running tasks.

flashcards.front: Is the Agents SDK OpenAI-only?
flashcards.back: No. It is provider-agnostic: Responses, Chat Completions and many other LLM providers.

flashcards.front: First question before building an agent?
flashcards.back: Is a single call or a fixed workflow enough? Use the simplest design that meets the need.

flashcards.front: Agents SDK: default `max_turns`, and what happens when it is exceeded?
flashcards.back: 10. The run raises `MaxTurnsExceeded`. Passing `None` removes the limit.

flashcards.front: How does the model see a handoff in the Agents SDK?
flashcards.back: As a tool named `transfer_to_<agent_name>` (overridable with `tool_name_override`).

flashcards.front: Which `handoff()` option edits the history the next agent receives?
flashcards.back: `input_filter`, e.g. `handoff_filters.remove_all_tools`. Not supported with server-managed conversations.

flashcards.front: `tool_use_behavior` options on an SDK Agent?
flashcards.back: `"run_llm_again"` (default), `"stop_on_first_tool"`, `StopAtTools([...])`, or a custom function.

flashcards.front: What does `output_type` on an Agent do?
flashcards.back: Makes the final output a structured type instead of plain text; the run ends when the model produces it with no tool calls.

flashcards.front: Function tool raises an exception: default SDK behaviour?
flashcards.back: The error is reported to the model so it can recover. Set `failure_error_function=None` to re-raise.

flashcards.front: What do SDK hosted tools (WebSearchTool, FileSearchTool, CodeInterpreterTool, HostedMCPTool) require?
flashcards.back: `OpenAIResponsesModel`: they run on OpenAI's side via the Responses API.

flashcards.front: Which agent do input and output guardrails run on?
flashcards.back: Input: only the first agent. Output: only the last agent. Tool guardrails wrap function tools (not handoffs or hosted tools).

flashcards.front: Input guardrails: parallel or blocking?
flashcards.back: Parallel with the agent by default; `run_in_parallel=False` makes the agent wait for the check.

flashcards.front: What happens when a guardrail's `tripwire_triggered` is true?
flashcards.back: The run stops with an exception such as `InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` or `OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered`.

flashcards.front: SDK approval flow, in order?
flashcards.back: `needs_approval` on the tool → run pauses with `result.interruptions` → `result.to_state()` → `state.approve()`/`reject()` → `Runner.run(agent, state)`.

flashcards.front: Is a deserialised `RunState` trusted?
flashcards.back: No. `from_json` does not authenticate; load only snapshots you stored and trust.

flashcards.front: Does approving a tool call guarantee it executes exactly once?
flashcards.back: No. Use idempotency keys for payments and other consequential actions.

flashcards.front: Name four Agents SDK session backends.
flashcards.back: Any of: SQLiteSession, RedisSession, SQLAlchemySession, OpenAIConversationsSession, OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession, EncryptedSession.

flashcards.front: Can a session be combined with `previous_response_id` or `conversation_id`?
flashcards.back: No. Choose one state mechanism; `conversation_id` and `previous_response_id` are also mutually exclusive.

flashcards.front: Agents SDK tracing defaults?
flashcards.back: On by default; `trace_include_sensitive_data` defaults to True. Disable with `OPENAI_AGENTS_DISABLE_TRACING=1`, `set_tracing_disabled(True)` or `RunConfig.tracing_disabled`.

flashcards.front: Agents SDK tracing and Zero Data Retention?
flashcards.back: Tracing is unavailable for ZDR organisations.

flashcards.front: How do you start work in the Agents API (beta)?
flashcards.back: Create a session, e.g. `client.beta.agents.sessions.create`, with a model, tools, an environment and input.

flashcards.front: How does the Agents API run subagents, and what does it cost?
flashcards.back: In parallel (`multi_agent.enabled`, `max_concurrent_subagents`). No extra fee: you pay for tokens and tools.

flashcards.front: Status of Agent Builder (AgentKit)?
flashcards.back: Deprecated, shutting down at the end of November 2026. Build in code (SDK or Agents API); ChatKit remains available.

flashcards.front: How does OpenAI prompt caching work?
flashcards.back: It is automatic and on by default. It reuses a repeated prompt prefix once the prompt passes a minimum length (1,024 tokens on current models). Cached input is cheaper and faster, and outputs don't change.

flashcards.front: What breaks prompt caching?
flashcards.back: Any change in the prefix, e.g. a timestamp or user name at the top of the instructions.

flashcards.front: When use the Batch API?
flashcards.back: Offline work nobody is waiting on: back-fills, bulk extraction, offline eval runs. 50% cheaper, with a 24-hour completion window.

flashcards.front: What is background mode for?
flashcards.back: Long-running responses: set background: true, then poll while the status is queued or in_progress (or cancel), instead of holding a connection open.

flashcards.front: Errors to retry with backoff?
flashcards.back: 429 (rate limit) and 5xx. Use exponential backoff with jitter and treat Retry-After as a minimum wait.

flashcards.front: Should you retry a 400?
flashcards.back: No. Fix the request. The same goes for quota or billing errors.

flashcards.front: Levers to fit more work under rate limits?
flashcards.back: Shorter prompts, a tight max_output_tokens (it feeds the TPM estimate), lower reasoning effort, and moving offline work to Batch (separate pool).

flashcards.front: Most reliable grader type?
flashcards.back: Code-based checks (exact match, schema, unit tests) when the answer is checkable.

flashcards.front: How to trust an LLM-as-judge?
flashcards.back: Give it a clear rubric and calibrate it against human-labelled samples.

flashcards.front: When to run your eval set?
flashcards.back: Before choosing a model, on every prompt, tool or model change (ideally in CI), and on sampled production traffic.

flashcards.front: Fine-tuning or retrieval for changing facts?
flashcards.back: Retrieval (or tools). Fine-tuning bakes in a snapshot; use it for stable behaviour on narrow tasks.

flashcards.front: Common reason to fine-tune?
flashcards.back: A smaller, cheaper model matching a larger one on a stable, narrow task with many examples. Caveat: OpenAI fine-tuning is closed to new users and winding down.

flashcards.front: How do you match Batch API results to inputs?
flashcards.back: By custom_id. The output order may differ from the input order.

flashcards.front: What happens to a Batch job that hits its 24h window?
flashcards.back: Completed results are kept (and billed). Unfinished requests get a batch_expired error; resubmit only those.

flashcards.front: Where do you see prompt cache hits?
flashcards.back: usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens in the response.

flashcards.front: Do cached tokens count toward TPM limits?
flashcards.back: Yes. Caching cuts cost and latency but not rate-limit usage.

flashcards.front: What is service_tier "flex"?
flashcards.back: A beta tier with Batch-level pricing for synchronous requests. It is slower and may return an uncharged 429 Resource Unavailable; retry or fall back to the default tier (auto).

flashcards.front: Why not add your own retry loop around the official SDK?
flashcards.back: The SDKs already auto-retry 429 and 503. Stacked retries multiply traffic, and failed requests still count toward limits.

flashcards.front: What is the status of OpenAI's hosted Evals platform?
flashcards.back: Deprecated: read-only since 2026-10-31, shutting down 2026-11-30. The named replacements are Promptfoo and Datasets. Hosted graders are deprecated too.

flashcards.front: Can a new organization start fine-tuning on OpenAI today?
flashcards.back: No. Fine-tuning closed to new users on 2026-05-07. Active existing customers can create jobs until 2027-01-06.

flashcards.front: Direct vs indirect prompt injection?
flashcards.back: Direct: the user overrides instructions. Indirect: instructions hidden in documents, web pages or tool results.

flashcards.front: Single best defence against prompt injection?
flashcards.back: There isn't one: layer least privilege, approvals, treating content as data, output validation and monitoring.

flashcards.front: What does the moderation endpoint do?
flashcards.back: Classifies text and images for harm categories (via the free omni-moderation-latest model) so you can screen input and output.

flashcards.front: Where must API keys live?
flashcards.back: Server-side, in env vars or a secrets manager; never in browser or mobile code.

flashcards.front: Key hygiene practices?
flashcards.back: Separate keys/projects per environment, restricted permissions, rotation, usage limits.

flashcards.front: How to avoid storing responses server-side?
flashcards.back: Set `store=false` and manage history yourself; review data controls and retention terms.

flashcards.front: Safeguards for computer use or shell tools?
flashcards.back: Sandboxes, restricted network/file access, turn and spend caps, human approval for irreversible steps.

flashcards.front: Why minimise personal data in prompts?
flashcards.back: Less exposure and easier compliance; send only what the task needs.

flashcards.front: Where should untrusted data go: developer or user messages?
flashcards.back: User messages. Never put untrusted data in developer messages, which carry higher authority.

flashcards.front: How do structured outputs reduce prompt-injection risk in multi-step agents?
flashcards.back: Enums and fixed schemas between steps leave no freeform channel for injected instructions to pass through.

flashcards.front: omni-moderation-latest: cost and inputs?
flashcards.back: Free; classifies text and images (not audio).

flashcards.front: Key fields in a moderation result?
flashcards.back: `flagged`, `categories`, `category_scores` (0 to 1) and `category_applied_input_types`.

flashcards.front: What is a safety identifier?
flashcards.back: A hashed per-user ID sent with requests so misuse can be tied to one end user without sharing personal data.

flashcards.front: Default retention for Responses API response objects?
flashcards.back: Stored for 30 days by default; set `store: false` to disable. ZDR orgs run stateless.

flashcards.front: How does remote MCP approval work in the Responses API?
flashcards.back: On by default: the model emits `mcp_approval_request`; you send `mcp_approval_response` in a new request. One approval covers one call.

flashcards.front: Is a deserialized RunState trusted?
flashcards.back: No. `from_json` does not authenticate the snapshot; load only from trusted storage.

flashcards.front: Why use idempotency keys with approved tool calls?
flashcards.back: Approval does not guarantee exactly-once execution, so retries could repeat side effects.

flashcards.front: Agents SDK tracing and sensitive data?
flashcards.back: Tracing is on by default and `trace_include_sensitive_data` defaults to True; it is unavailable for ZDR orgs.

questions.stem: A team is starting a new OpenAI integration in November 2026. Which API surface should they build on?
options: The Responses API
The Assistants API
The legacy Completions API
The Batch API for every request
questions.explanation: The docs say that while Chat Completions remains supported, Responses is recommended for all new projects. The Assistants API was sunset on 2026-08-26, and Batch is only for offline jobs.
rationales: Correct: the docs recommend Responses for all new projects.
Sunset on 2026-08-26 and no longer available.
Legacy text completion; not the place for new agentic features.
Batch is asynchronous and only for offline work.

sources.title: Migrate to Responses — OpenAI API docs

questions.stem:
What does this code print?

```python
resp = client.responses.create(model=MODEL, input="Hi")
print(type(resp.output))
```
options: A single string with the answer
A dict of token counts
A stream iterator
A list of output items
questions.explanation: `response.output` is an array of items (messages, reasoning, tool calls). The joined text is available via the `output_text` convenience, and token counts are in `usage`.
rationales: Correct: output is an array of typed items.

questions.stem: Your chat UI feels slow: users stare at a spinner for 6 seconds before any text appears. Total cost is fine. What is the best first change?
options: Raise max_output_tokens
Resend the whole history twice for reliability
Stream the response and render text deltas as they arrive
Switch to the Batch API
questions.explanation: Streaming improves perceived latency because text appears as it is generated. It does not reduce total work, but the user sees progress immediately.
rationales: More output tokens do not make the first token arrive sooner.
Correct: streaming cuts time to first token.
Batch is asynchronous and makes interactive latency far worse.

questions.stem: A developer chains turns with `previous_response_id` and assumes the 40-turn conversation now costs the same per turn as turn one. What is wrong with that assumption?
options: Nothing; chaining makes old turns free
All prior input tokens in the chain are still billed as input on each turn
previous_response_id only works for 5 turns
Chained responses are billed at the Batch rate
questions.explanation: Chaining spares you resending earlier turns, but the docs state that all previous input tokens in the chain are billed as input. Long chats should be compacted or summarised.
rationales: There is no such fixed limit stated.
Chaining does not change the pricing tier.

questions.stem: A health-tech company must not keep any model responses on OpenAI's servers beyond the request. How should they manage conversation state?
options: Set store=false and send the conversation history themselves each turn
Use the Conversations API
Chain with previous_response_id
Use default settings; responses expire after 30 days
questions.explanation: With `store=false` responses are not saved, so the app must manage history itself. Chaining and Conversations both depend on server-side storage (also review data-retention agreements).
rationales: Correct: no server-side storage; manual history.
Default storage is exactly what they must avoid.

questions.stem: Which use case fits the Conversations API best?
options: A one-shot classification request
A request that must never be stored
Lowering token cost by skipping history
A user continues the same thread from phone, laptop and a nightly job
questions.explanation: The Conversations API gives a durable conversation object with its own ID, designed for state reused across sessions, devices or jobs.
rationales: Correct: durable state across sessions and devices.

questions.stem: An app uses a reasoning model with manual history. After a few turns quality drops and the model seems to forget earlier analysis. The code appends only the assistant's final text to the history. What is the likely fix?
options: Switch to JSON mode
Add "remember everything" to the instructions
Append every output item, including reasoning items, to the next input
Lower the reasoning effort
questions.explanation: For reasoning models the docs recommend replaying all output items, including reasoning items, so context carries forward. Dropping them loses the model's earlier work.
rationales: Correct: the docs say to replay all output items for reasoning models.

questions.stem: A classification endpoint is accurate but expensive on a flagship reasoning model. What should the team try first?
options: Switch to the Assistants API
Run their eval set on lower reasoning effort and a smaller model, and keep the cheapest that passes
Fine-tune immediately
Raise temperature to finish faster
questions.explanation: The cheapest model and lowest reasoning effort that pass your evals is the right setting. Measure rather than guess; fine-tuning comes later if needed.
rationales: The Assistants API was sunset and is unrelated to cost.
Does not reduce cost meaningfully and hurts consistency.

questions.stem: Where should stable, system-level rules for the assistant go in a Responses API call?
options: In the instructions parameter
In max_output_tokens
In the model name
In the metadata field only
questions.explanation: The `instructions` parameter (or a developer message) carries system-level guidance and takes priority over `input`. Note that it applies only to the current request.
rationales: Metadata is not shown to the model as rules.

sources.title: Migrate to Responses — OpenAI API docs

questions.stem: Why should model IDs like `gpt-6-astra` live in configuration rather than being hard-coded across the codebase? (Select two.)
options: You can run the eval suite against a new model by changing one setting
Hard-coded IDs are rejected by the API
Configuration makes requests cheaper
Model lineups change often, so upgrades become a single change
questions.explanation: Model names and tiers change frequently. Keeping them in config makes upgrades and A/B comparisons a one-line change backed by an eval run.
rationales: Location of the string does not affect price.

questions.stem: What is true about reasoning tokens on GPT reasoning models?
options: They only appear with stream=True
They are billed as cached input
They are billed (as output tokens) even though you do not see all of them
They are free
questions.explanation: Reasoning tokens count toward output billing and latency, which is why lower reasoning effort is a cost lever for simple tasks.

questions.stem: A team maintains an older integration built on the Assistants API. What is its status in November 2026?
options: Only available through Batch
Sunset on 2026-08-26 and no longer available; migrate to the Responses API
The recommended API for new agents
Renamed to the Agents API
questions.explanation: OpenAI sunset the Assistants API on 2026-08-26 and it is no longer available. The migration guide moves Threads to Conversations, Runs to Responses and Run steps to Items.
rationales: The Agents API is a different, managed harness launched in 2026.

sources.title: Migrate to Responses — OpenAI API docs

questions.stem: A hotel wants a speech-to-speech front-desk assistant with natural, low-latency conversation. Which API is the best fit?
options: The Realtime API with a realtime speech-to-speech model
The Batch API with text-to-speech
Chat Completions with polling every second
File search over audio files
questions.explanation: The Realtime API is built for low-latency speech-to-speech sessions, and the Models page lists dedicated voice models (GPT-Live and the gpt-realtime family). Verify current voice model IDs in the docs.
rationales: Correct: built for low-latency speech-to-speech sessions.

questions.stem: A developer switches a triage call to `gpt-6-astra` and, to cut cost, sends `reasoning: {"effort": "none"}`. Every request now fails with HTTP 400. What is the best fix?
options: Retry with exponential backoff; the 400 is transient
Use an effort value the model supports (for example `low`), or move to a model such as GPT-6.1 Terra or GPT-6 Luna that supports `none`
Remove `reasoning` and set `temperature: 0` instead
Move the effort setting into `instructions`
questions.explanation: Supported effort values differ by model, and GPT-6 Astra rejects `none` with a 400. Pick a supported value, or for a cheap, low-thinking task choose a model that supports `none`. A 400 is a request error, so retrying cannot help.
rationales: A 400 is a client error; retrying the same request fails again.
Correct: match the effort value to the model's supported list, or pick a model that offers `none`.
Temperature is not a substitute for effort and does not address the invalid value.
Instructions are prompt text; they do not configure reasoning effort.

questions.stem: A summarizer on a reasoning model sets `max_output_tokens: 400` because summaries are short. Some responses come back with an empty `output_text` and `status: "incomplete"`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The cap counts reasoning tokens too, so the model spent the budget thinking before writing any visible text
The content filter removed the summary
`output_text` is only populated when streaming
The model ignores `max_output_tokens` and the API truncated the input instead
questions.explanation: On reasoning models `max_output_tokens` covers reasoning plus visible output. When the budget runs out the response is `incomplete` with reason `max_output_tokens`, sometimes with no visible text. Raise the cap (or lower effort) and check `status` and `incomplete_details` in code.
rationales: Correct: reasoning consumed the cap; the incomplete reason would be `max_output_tokens`.
Possible in general, but the incomplete reason would then be `content_filter`, and the tight cap is the obvious cause here.
The cap applies to output, not input, and the model does respect it.

questions.stem: A chat UI streams Responses API output. Users report that raw JSON fragments and odd status text sometimes appear in the chat bubble. The handler appends the payload of every event to the bubble. Which change is correct?
options: Disable streaming and poll the response every second
Append only `response.output_text.delta` text; handle `response.refusal.delta`, `error` and `response.completed` with their own logic
Switch to Chat Completions, which has only one event type
Parse every event as JSON and display it only if it parses
questions.explanation: Responses streaming uses typed semantic events. Only `response.output_text.delta` carries the visible text to render; other events signal lifecycle, refusals, function-call arguments or errors and need their own handling.
rationales: Throws away the perceived-latency benefit of streaming.
Correct: route by event type and render only text deltas.
Migrating backwards does not fix event handling, and Responses is the recommended API.
Function-call argument deltas and lifecycle events would still leak into the UI.

questions.stem: A bot sends `instructions` (tone, refund policy) on the first call only, then chains later turns with `previous_response_id`. From turn two onward it ignores the refund policy. What explains this?
options: previous_response_id drops the user's earlier messages
The policy must be put in `metadata` to persist
`instructions` apply only to the current request and are not carried forward by `previous_response_id`; send them on every call
Reasoning models ignore instructions after the first turn by design
questions.explanation: The docs state that `instructions` apply only to the current request; with `previous_response_id`, earlier instructions are not carried over. Sending the same instructions on each call fixes it (and a stable prefix also helps caching).
rationales: Earlier inputs and outputs are part of the chain; it is the instructions that are not carried.
Metadata is not shown to the model as guidance.
Correct per the text-generation and migration docs.
There is no such behavior; the instructions simply are not present.

questions.stem: A team is migrating a sunset Assistants API integration to the Responses API. Which mappings are correct? (Select two.)
options: Threads become Conversations
Runs become Batch jobs
Run steps become Items
Assistants become vector stores
questions.explanation: OpenAI's migration guide maps Assistants to Prompts, Threads to Conversations, Runs to Responses and Run steps to Items. Batch jobs and vector stores are unrelated concepts.
rationales: Runs become Responses; Batch is for offline jobs.
Assistants map to prompts (now kept in your code); vector stores are for file search.

questions.stem: A long-running research chat on a reasoning model keeps growing; each turn's input cost climbs and the context window is filling up. The org has a zero-data-retention requirement, so `store=false`. Which approaches fit? (Select two.)
options: Enable server-side compaction with `context_management` and a `compact_threshold`
Switch to `previous_response_id` chaining so old turns stop being billed
Call `/responses/compact` and pass the returned compaction item back unchanged in later input
Strip reasoning items from the replayed history and edit the compaction item to remove old content
questions.explanation: Compaction via `context_management` works with `store=false`, and the stateless `/responses/compact` endpoint returns an opaque encrypted item to pass back as-is. Chaining needs stored responses and still bills prior input tokens.
rationales: Correct: server-side compaction is ZDR-friendly with store=false.
Chaining depends on stored responses and still bills all prior input tokens.
Correct: the compaction item is opaque and should not be pruned.
Dropping reasoning items loses context, and the compaction item must not be edited.

questions.stem: Finance asks how much of a reasoning model's bill comes from hidden reasoning. Where should the team read this per request?
options: `usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens`
The length of `output_text`
`usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`
It cannot be measured because reasoning is hidden
questions.explanation: Reasoning tokens are not visible but are billed as output tokens, and the count is reported in `usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`. That makes it easy to compare effort levels.
rationales: That is cached input, a different cost line.
The count is reported in usage even though the content is hidden.

questions.stem: The model returns two `function_call` items in one response: `get_order(A-1)` and `get_order(B-2)`. What must your code send back?
options: One output containing only the first result
A new user message asking which order to check
Nothing; the model will retry automatically
Two function_call_output items, one per call_id
questions.explanation: Every function call needs a matching `function_call_output` with the same `call_id`. Parallel calls are normal; answer all of them.
rationales: The second call would be left unanswered.
The model already asked for both.

questions.stem: Which signal should end a function-calling loop?
options: A fixed count of three iterations
The response took longer than 2 seconds
The response contains no more function_call items
The text contains the word "done"
questions.explanation: Stop when the model stops requesting tools. Keep a max-turn cap as a safety net, not as the primary control.
rationales: A cap is a safety net, not the signal.

questions.stem: A tool call fails because the order ID does not exist. What is the best thing to return?
options: Retry the same call indefinitely
A structured error in the function_call_output, e.g. {"error": "order not found", "hint": "ask the user to confirm the ID"}
Raise an exception and end the request
An empty string
questions.explanation: Returning errors as data with a next step lets the model ask the user, try another approach or explain the failure, instead of crashing or looping.
rationales: A permanent error will not fix itself.
The model may misread it as success or no data.

questions.stem: Policy: refunds above $100 need a manager. The prompt says so, yet a jailbreak got a $900 refund issued. What is the right fix?
options: Enforce the limit inside issue_refund and require an approval step above $100
Repeat the rule three times in the instructions
Lower the temperature
Switch to a larger model
questions.explanation: Rules that must always hold belong in code (or approvals), not only in prompts. Prompts make compliance likely; code makes it certain.
rationales: Better models still are not a policy control.

questions.stem: Which `tool_choice` value forces the model to call some tool on this turn?
options: "auto"
"none"
"parallel"
"required"
questions.explanation: `required` forces one or more tool calls; `auto` lets the model choose; `none` disables tools; you can also force a named function or restrict to `allowed_tools`.

questions.stem: An agent keeps calling `search_orders` when it should call `search_invoices`. Both tools have one-line descriptions. What is the most effective fix?
options: Raise reasoning effort to maximum
Rename the tools to t1 and t2
Rewrite both descriptions to say what each covers, when to use it and when not to
Add a third tool that calls both
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the main signal the model uses to pick a tool. Clear scope, examples and "don't use for" notes fix most mis-selections.
rationales: Helps a little at a cost; ambiguity remains.

questions.stem: You need answers grounded in current public news with sources, and you do not want to build a scraper. What should you use?
options: Fine-tune on yesterday's news
The built-in web search tool
File search over a vector store
Code Interpreter
questions.explanation: The hosted web search tool retrieves current information and returns sources without you writing the retrieval loop.
rationales: Runs Python; not a search engine.
